name: Alfama
tagline: Lisbon's oldest quarter begins across the road from the cruise terminal

description.short: Lisbon's oldest district, Alfama is a captivating maze of narrow cobbled streets, colorful houses, and hidden courtyards that survived the 1755 earthquake. Home to traditional Fado music, vintage trams, and stunning viewpoints overlooking the Tagus River.
description.full:
Alfama is the one Lisbon sight you can reach without any transport: its lower lanes start across Avenida Infante Dom Henrique from the Jardim do Tabaco terminal, about 8 minutes on foot. The catch is the gradient. The district climbs from the river to the castle walls on stairs and steep cobbles, so decide which way you will walk before you set off.

The easiest plan for a port day is top-down. Take a taxi, a tuk-tuk or Tram 28E up to Largo das Portas do Sol, look at the view, then walk downhill through the lanes back towards the ship. Walking up and back down covers the same streets at roughly twice the effort.

With 90 minutes: the Portas do Sol and Santa Luzia viewpoints, which sit a minute or two apart, then a slow walk down to Largo do Chafariz de Dentro, where the Fado Museum stands a few minutes from the terminal. With three to four hours, add the Sé (Lisbon's cathedral, closed to visitors on Sundays) or Castelo de São Jorge higher up. On a Tuesday or Saturday, the Feira da Ladra flea market fills Campo de Santa Clara, on the eastern edge of the district.

On busy ship days, roughly 10:00 to 15:00 is when excursion groups crowd the viewpoints and Tram 28E arrives full. Early in your port day is calmer, and the side lanes away from the tram line stay quiet at almost any hour.

What to skip if time is tight: queuing for Tram 28E only for the ride, restaurants with touts and picture menus on the main routes, and trying to see every church. The lanes themselves are the point.

Alfama's irregular street plan predates the 1755 earthquake, which hit the flat Baixa far harder. People still live here, so keep voices down in the narrow residential alleys.
description.history: The name comes from the Arabic al-hamma, usually linked to the springs and baths of the area. Under Moorish rule this was the residential quarter below the citadel, and its tangle of alleys still follows that pattern. After Afonso Henriques took Lisbon in 1147, Alfama became home to fishermen, sailors and dockworkers. The 1755 earthquake devastated much of the city, but Alfama's rocky hillside fared better than the low-lying Baixa, which is why its medieval layout survives instead of the grid rebuilt downtown. In the 19th century fado took shape in the taverns of Alfama and neighbouring Mouraria, which is why the Fado Museum stands at its foot. Each June the Santo António festivities fill its streets with grills and music.
description.significance: Alfama is the largest surviving piece of pre-earthquake Lisbon: irregular streets, small squares and stairways that show how the city looked before its planned 18th-century rebuild. For a cruise passenger it is also practical. The terminal sits at its foot, and the cathedral, the castle and the two main viewpoints are inside or on the edge of the district, so one walk covers several of the city's main sights.

directions.general: Located on the hillside between Castelo de São Jorge and the Tagus River, east of downtown Baixa district
directions.fromCruisePort: Alfama starts across the road from the Jardim do Tabaco cruise terminal: about 450 m and 8 minutes on foot to the lower lanes. Everything above that is uphill on stairs and cobbles; if you want the views without the climb, take a taxi or tuk-tuk to Largo das Portas do Sol and walk down.
directions.publicTransport: Tram 28E traverses Alfama (iconic route). Metro to Santa Apolónia or Terreiro do Paço, then walk uphill. Buses 734, 737 serve upper Alfama near castle. From Baixa, steep 15-20 minute uphill walk.
directions.parking: Not recommended to drive - extremely narrow medieval streets. Limited parking at Santa Apolónia. Park elsewhere and walk/take tram.

admissionPrices.notes: Free to walk around. Paid sights in or next to Alfama include Castelo de São Jorge (€17), the Sé (€7) and the Fado Museum (€5). Tram 28E on-board fare €3.30 (Carris, 2026).

visitingInformation.bestTimeToVisit: Early morning (8-10am) for fewer tourists and authentic neighborhood life. Late afternoon for golden light and sunset from viewpoints. Tuesday or Saturday morning for Feira da Ladra flea market. Avoid midday summer heat.
visitingInformation.adviceForVisitors: Wear comfortable walking shoes - very steep, uneven cobblestones and many stairs. Getting lost is part of the charm - embrace it, but keep heading downhill to reach waterfront. Start at top (castle or Graça) and walk down rather than exhausting uphill climb. Watch for pickpockets on crowded Tram 28E. Visit Feira da Ladra flea market Tuesday/Saturday morning. Experience authentic Fado dinner at traditional restaurant (avoid tourist traps with touts). Respect residents - it's a real neighborhood, not a theme park. Bring water. Best explored on foot, not by car. Allow 3-4 hours minimum for meaningful exploration.

cruisePassengerInfo.timeNeededFromPort: 1.5–4 hours: 90 minutes covers the two viewpoints and a walk down; allow half a day to add the cathedral or the castle
cruisePassengerInfo.accessibility: The lower lanes are about 8 minutes' flat walk from the terminal; everything above is steep cobbles and stairs. Visitors with limited mobility can take a taxi to Largo das Portas do Sol, where the viewpoint is at street level.
combinableWith: Portas do Sol and Santa Luzia viewpoints
tips: Go up by transport and walk down: a taxi, tuk-tuk or Tram 28E to Largo das Portas do Sol saves the steepest climb, and the way back to the terminal is downhill.
Tram 28E costs €3.30 per trip if you pay on board (Carris 2026 fare). A Carris/Metro single on a Navegante card costs €1.90 and can be bought at Santa Apolónia metro station.
The Fado Museum at Largo do Chafariz de Dentro is the closest paid sight to the ship: Tuesday to Sunday 10:00–18:00 (last entry 17:30), adult €5, closed on Mondays.
Feira da Ladra runs on Tuesdays and Saturdays, 09:00–18:00, at Campo de Santa Clara behind São Vicente de Fora.
The viewpoints and Tram 28E are at their fullest between about 10:00 and 15:00 on busy ship days; go early in your port day if you can.
Street names are on small tiled plaques at corners and many lanes end in stairs or dead ends; download an offline map before leaving the ship.
Pickpockets work Tram 28E and the viewpoint railings; keep bags closed and in front of you.
Allow 20–30 minutes to get back to the terminal from the top of Alfama: the walk is short on the map, but the lanes are slow and easy to get lost in.

highlights: Miradouro das Portas do Sol and Miradouro de Santa Luzia, side by side
Tram 28E and 12E climbing through Largo das Portas do Sol
Fado Museum at Largo do Chafariz de Dentro, a few minutes from the terminal
Sé de Lisboa, the city's cathedral, on the western edge
Castelo de São Jorge on the hilltop above
Feira da Ladra flea market at Campo de Santa Clara (Tuesday and Saturday)
Pre-1755 street plan of alleys, stairways and small squares
Panteão Nacional and São Vicente de Fora on the eastern ridge
Santo António festivities in the streets every June
facilities: Fado houses for live music performances

accessibility.mobilityNotes: NOT wheelchair accessible - extremely steep hills, narrow cobblestone streets, and countless staircases make Alfama very challenging for people with mobility issues. Lower waterfront areas somewhat more accessible. Tram 28E has limited wheelchair access. Consider taxi to upper viewpoints if mobility is an issue.
